posts.title: Talent Pool Software: How to Rank Your Own Database Before You Pay a Job Portal
posts.metaTitle: Talent Pool Software: Rank Your Own Database First
posts.description: We audited 3 million candidate records at one staffing firm: 10% duplicates, 10% junk, 80% still relevant. Portal spend fell from $100 a role to $60.
posts.dek: We audited 3 million candidate records sitting in one firm's Google Drive folders. A tenth were duplicates, a tenth were junk, and 80% were unique profiles nobody had touched in years.
posts.cardImageAlt: Sortinghat evaluation panel: a candidate scored 96, split into weighted criteria with a percentage and written justification for each

faq.q: What is talent pool software?
faq.a: Talent pool software consolidates, refreshes and ranks the candidates a staffing firm has already sourced, so recruiters can search their own database before paying to source externally. It differs from an ATS record store in that the pool is actively kept current and scored against live roles, rather than passively archived.

faq.q: How much of an old staffing database is still usable?
faq.a: In our audit of 3 million candidate records at one firm, about 10% were duplicates and about 10% held no usable company information. The remaining 80% were unique, real profiles that were out of date rather than worthless. Your own split will differ, and a sample audit of 500 records is the only reliable way to know it.

faq.q: Does database-first sourcing replace job portals like Naukri?
faq.a: No. It reduces how often you need them. Genuinely new skill requirements, new geographies and roles you have never worked still justify a fresh portal pull. The change is that these become the exception rather than the default on every role. In our customer data, job portal spend fell from roughly $100 per role to $60.

faq.q: How is candidate scoring different from keyword matching?
faq.a: Keyword matching checks whether terms appear in a CV. Scoring weighs the whole profile against the role's criteria and shows the reasoning behind each part of the result, so a recruiter can verify it rather than trust it blindly.

faq.q: What should you do with duplicate candidate records?
faq.a: Merge rather than delete, and only with a tool that preserves notes, call history, attachments and submission history from every source record. A merge that loses the 2023 note explaining why a client rejected someone will cost you that client's trust when you submit them again.

faq.q: How long can a staffing firm keep candidate data?
faq.a: Retention has to be defensible rather than indefinite. India's DPDP Act and the GDPR both require a lawful basis for holding personal data and a stated retention position. Records with no reachable contact, no placement history and no recent activity are usually a compliance exposure rather than an asset.

posts.title: Hiring Scorecards: How to Turn a Job Description Into Weighted Evaluation Criteria
posts.metaTitle: Hiring Scorecards: Turn a JD Into Weighted Criteria
posts.description: A real hiring scorecard built from one job description, with the eight criteria and their actual weights, and why one candidate scores differently at two firms.
posts.dek: A job description tells candidates about the role. A hiring scorecard tells your team who to reject, and why. Here is one built from a real job description, with the actual weights.
posts.cardImageAlt: Sortinghat job description review: a parsed Director of Engineering role beside structured fields for client, salary and location

toc.label: Why a JD is not a scorecard
How to build your first one

faq.q: What is a hiring scorecard?
faq.a: A structured definition of who qualifies for a role, made up of evaluation criteria, a scoring guideline for each, and a weight reflecting how much each one matters. Candidates are rated against every criterion and the final score is the weighted average, which lets a team evaluate consistently rather than relying on each recruiter's reading of a job description.

faq.q: How is a hiring scorecard different from a job description?
faq.a: A job description is written for candidates and describes the role attractively enough that someone applies. A scorecard is written for the hiring team and defines the decision rule, including what disqualifies someone. One is a sales document, the other is criteria.

faq.q: How do you weight hiring criteria?
faq.a: By asking what the role actually risks failing on, not by what sounds most impressive. On a site-lead hire, team building and operational skills should outweigh specialist technical knowledge, because building the team is the job. Weights of 1 to 5 across six to ten criteria is a workable range.

faq.q: Can the same candidate score differently for the same role at two companies?
faq.a: They should. Same job title does not mean same job. If the criteria and weights reflect what each company actually needs, including company stage and size, the same profile will score differently against each, and that difference is the useful part.

faq.q: How long does it take to build a hiring scorecard?
faq.a: The criteria generate from the job description in one step. The part worth spending time on is adjusting the weights and adding the rules the client believes but did not write down, which is usually a fifteen to thirty minute conversation.

faq.q: How do you test a hiring scorecard before using it?
faq.a: Score two people whose outcome you already know: one you would definitely hire and one you clearly rejected. If the scorecard cannot separate them, it is not measuring the job yet. Adjusting it against three known CVs is far cheaper than discovering the problem after three weeks of submissions.

posts.title: AI Screening Calls: What Gets Asked, Verified and Written to the Record
posts.metaTitle: AI Screening Calls: What They Verify and Capture
posts.description: 70% of candidates complete an AI screening call in 3 to 7 minutes. What it verifies, which CV claims collapse under it, and what reaches the record.
posts.dek: Roughly 70% of candidates complete an AI screening call, and it takes three to seven minutes. Here is what the call is for, which CV claims collapse under it, and what lands on the record afterwards.
posts.cardImageAlt: Sortinghat activity timeline: an automatically logged call written to the candidate record with the stage move attached

faq.q: What is an AI screening call?
faq.a: A structured, automated phone conversation that qualifies a candidate against a specific role: confirming interest, availability, compensation expectation, and the CV claims that matter most for that role. It typically runs three to seven minutes and writes its findings onto the candidate record as structured data rather than as an audio file.

faq.q: Do candidates complete AI screening calls?
faq.a: In our data, around 70% do, with a typical call lasting three to seven minutes. Completion is a real quality metric rather than a vanity one: a call people abandon is selecting for patience, and the candidates most likely to hang up are the ones with the most options.

faq.q: Do candidates have to be told they are speaking to an AI?
faq.a: Yes, in a growing number of jurisdictions. The EU AI Act classifies recruitment AI as high-risk with obligations that took effect on 2 August 2026, and several US states including Illinois have their own disclosure rules for automated hiring tools. Beyond compliance, undisclosed automated calls damage candidate trust for very little gain.

faq.q: Can an AI screening call reject a candidate?
faq.a: It should not. Under the EU AI Act, human oversight of automated decisions is required for high-risk systems, which includes recruitment. Good practice and current regulation point the same way: the AI ranks and flags, a person decides.

faq.q: Is candidate data from AI screening calls used to train models?
faq.a: Not in our case. Call data is stored encrypted, belongs to the client whose candidate it is, and is neither used for model training nor shared with third parties. There is no pooled dataset across customers. Ask any vendor this question directly and expect a one-sentence answer.

faq.q: Which CV claims most often fail verification on a screening call?
faq.a: Quantified impact claims. Percentage improvements, and revenue or GMV figures presented as moving from one number to another. When the call asks a second question about the baseline, the time period or the individual contribution, candidates who did the work answer immediately and those who did not become vague.

posts.title: Natural Language Candidate Search: Five Real Queries, and Why Vague Ones Fail
posts.metaTitle: Natural Language Candidate Search: 5 Real Queries
posts.description: Five real natural language searches run on a live staffing database, what they returned, and the one reason most candidate search queries disappoint.
posts.dek: Real searches run against a live staffing database, the results they returned, and the single reason most natural language queries disappoint the person typing them.
posts.cardImageAlt: Sortinghat search: a natural language query for engineers in Bangalore returning 71 ranked candidates

toc.label: Your own database, not the web
How to test on your own data

faq.q: What is natural language candidate search?
faq.a: Search that takes a plain-language description of the person you want and returns ranked matches, without Boolean operators or manually built filters. It interprets meaning rather than matching keywords, which lets it handle conditions like company stage or institution tier that never appear as literal terms on a CV.

faq.q: Is natural language search better than Boolean search for recruiting?
faq.a: For compound queries and conditions that are judgements rather than keywords, yes. For exact-match requirements such as a specific certification number or a named employer, a filter remains more precise. Most real recruiting searches are the first kind.

faq.q: Why is my natural language candidate search returning poor results?
faq.a: Almost always because the query describes a category rather than a person. A query like 'backend engineer in Bangalore with four years of experience' has three conditions and thousands of matches. Add the specific stack, the institution tier and the domain context, and the result set changes completely.

faq.q: Does natural language search cover LinkedIn and job boards?
faq.a: In our case it searches your own database only. External sourcing is a separate motion with a separate licence cost, and the sensible order is to exhaust what you already own before paying to search elsewhere.

faq.q: Do recruiters still need to learn Boolean search?
faq.a: It remains useful on platforms that only support it, so it has not disappeared. It is no longer a sensible criterion for hiring a sourcer, because describing a profile precisely is now the scarce skill and it is far quicker to teach.

faq.q: How do you write a good candidate search query?
faq.a: Include four elements every time: the capability in detail, the level as a range, the hard constraints such as location and institution, and the context you would actually reject someone over, such as industry or company stage. Queries missing two of these are the ones that disappoint.

faq.a: It runs inside your browser on profiles you open yourself, reads the publicly visible sections of the page you are already viewing, and lets you save that person into your own database against a job or a company. It works at the pace you browse, because it is reading your session rather than running its own automated collection.

faq.q: What candidate data does a LinkedIn sourcing extension collect?
faq.a: Publicly visible profile information: work experience, education, skills and the About section. It does not collect private fields, connection graphs, message content, or anything behind a paid tier you do not hold.

faq.q: Do candidates need to be told their profile is in a recruiter's database?
faq.a: Under the GDPR, the UK regime and India's DPDP Act, notice obligations apply to personal data you hold, including data gathered without direct contact. Our platform can run notice campaigns over email, WhatsApp or call, but they are not enabled by default. Firms placing into the EU or UK should enable them and take their own legal advice on wording and timing.

faq.q: How long is sourced candidate data retained?
faq.a: For as long as the client remains on the platform, after which it is removed. Data is isolated per client, is not pooled across customers, is not used for model training, and is not shared with third parties.

faq.q: Is sourced candidate data used to train AI models?
faq.a: No. There is no cross-customer training set and no secondary use of client data. This is a question worth asking every vendor you evaluate, and worth being suspicious of any answer that takes more than a sentence.

faq.q: Is scraping LinkedIn profiles legal for recruiters?
faq.a: The position depends on jurisdiction, on the platform's own terms, and on how the data is collected, stored and used. What matters legally is the basis on which you process personal data rather than the label attached to the method. Ask any vendor to state, in writing, what they collect, where the collection happens, and on what basis.

posts.title: Staffing KPIs: The Four Numbers a Firm Owner Should Check Every Day
posts.metaTitle: Staffing KPIs: The 4 Numbers to Check Every Day
posts.description: Fill rate and time-to-fill are lagging indicators. The 4 staffing KPIs that move first, how to read each one when it falls, and the 10-minute daily routine.
posts.dek: Fill rate and time-to-fill are outcomes. By the time they move, the decision that caused them is six weeks old. Four numbers move earlier, and together they predict next month's revenue closely enough to act on.
posts.cardImageAlt: Staffing pipeline with candidates across stage columns, each showing a match score of 96, 93 or 92

toc.label: Why fill rate is the wrong daily number
What to do when one moves
Where four numbers is not enough

faq.q: What KPIs should a staffing agency track daily?
faq.a: Live submissions, interviews scheduled, offers in play, and receivables past 60 days. These are leading indicators that can still be influenced. Fill rate, time-to-fill and gross margin are lagging and belong in weekly or monthly reviews rather than a daily check.

faq.q: What is the difference between leading and lagging recruitment metrics?
faq.a: Leading metrics predict future outcomes and can still be changed by acting today. Lagging metrics report results that are already determined. Most recruitment dashboards are built almost entirely from lagging metrics, which is why they feel informative but rarely change anyone's behaviour.

faq.q: Why is time-to-fill a poor daily metric?
faq.a: It is measured from a start point you often do not control to an end point the client controls. A slow client can double it while your team does everything right. Checked daily it produces anxiety rather than decisions, and it moves on noise.

faq.q: How do you forecast staffing revenue from pipeline?
faq.a: Take offers in play, apply your own historical offer-to-join rate, and add stage-weighted values from earlier pipeline. Accuracy depends entirely on using your own conversion rates rather than industry averages, because conversion varies more by firm than by market.

faq.q: What does a falling submission-to-interview ratio mean?
faq.a: That the team is busy and the work is not landing. Pull the last ten rejections and read the reasons. If they cluster around one requirement, the brief was wrong. If they scatter, the screening was. It is the most expensive failure mode in staffing because it burns capacity without producing anything.

faq.q: Why should recruiters see receivables?
faq.a: Because the recruiter holds the relationship that unblocks the payment. Most overdue invoices in staffing are stuck on a query that one conversation resolves, and finance does not have the relationship to make that call.

posts.title: Recruiter Admin Time: Where the Hours Actually Go, and What Automatic Capture Removes
posts.metaTitle: Recruiter Admin Time: Where the Hours Actually Go
posts.description: A candidate's history lives across 5 channels and the record holds one. What recruiter admin costs, and what automatic capture must produce to remove it.
posts.dek: A candidate's history lives across five channels. The record holds whichever one the recruiter remembered to log. Here is what that costs and what automatic capture has to produce to fix it.
posts.cardImageAlt: Candidate record showing experience, location, full career timeline and channel actions for call, WhatsApp, LinkedIn and email

toc.label: Why the record is never current
How to measure your admin load

faq.q: How much time do recruiters spend on admin?
faq.a: Industry reporting consistently puts non-recruiting work at the majority of a recruiter's week, covering data entry, logging calls, updating stages and rebuilding context. The only number that matters for your firm is the one you measure on your own team, which takes one unannounced day of time tracking across three recruiters.

faq.q: What is automated call logging in a recruitment CRM?
faq.a: It captures conversations across phone, email, WhatsApp and LinkedIn and writes them onto the candidate record without anyone typing. The useful version extracts structured fields such as notice period and compensation, rather than only storing a transcript that somebody still has to read.

faq.q: What is the difference between a transcript and structured capture?
faq.a: A transcript is the words that were said. Structured capture pulls the facts out of those words into fields that can be searched, filtered and reported on. Only the second one saves time, because a transcript on a record still requires a human to read it before the record is usable.

faq.q: Does automated call logging require candidate consent?
faq.a: Recording consent rules vary by jurisdiction. India, several US states and the EU all impose requirements, and some require disclosure before recording begins. If your desks place across borders, the requirement is set by the candidate's location rather than your office's.

faq.q: Why is WhatsApp integration important for recruitment in India?
faq.a: In India, WhatsApp is often the primary channel candidates actually reply on. A system that does not thread WhatsApp into the candidate record will always hold an incomplete history, because the most current part of the conversation sits on an individual recruiter's phone.

faq.q: What should a delivery manager be able to see without asking anyone?
faq.a: The true state of every desk: which candidates were contacted, what they said, which submissions are live and where each one is stuck. If that requires a status meeting to establish, the logging is not working and the meeting is compensating for it.

posts.title: Candidate Response Rates by Channel: Call, WhatsApp and Email Compared
posts.metaTitle: Candidate Response Rates: Call vs WhatsApp vs Email
posts.description: Out of 100 candidates contacted for a strong role, about 40 respond to a call, 25 on WhatsApp and 12 to 15 by email. What that means for your sequence.
posts.dek: Out of 100 candidates contacted for a strong role: about 40 respond to a call, 25 on WhatsApp, and 12 to 15 by email. Here is what that means for how you sequence outreach.
posts.cardImageAlt: Candidate record header showing direct call, WhatsApp, LinkedIn and email actions alongside experience and location

toc.label: What the numbers do not tell you

faq.q: What is a good candidate response rate?
faq.a: In our own outreach on well-paid, credible roles, roughly 40 out of 100 people respond to a phone call, 25 respond on WhatsApp and 12 to 15 respond by email. Weaker roles perform materially worse on every channel, so treat these as a ceiling rather than an average.

faq.q: Which channel gets the highest response from candidates?
faq.a: The phone, by a clear margin, followed by WhatsApp and then email. This surprises teams who assume messaging has replaced calling. A call is harder to ignore and easier to answer in thirty seconds, and it carries an implicit signal that the role is worth a person's time.

faq.q: How many times should you follow up with a candidate?
faq.a: Four touches across roughly ten days, changing the channel each time. Beyond that, additional messages damage your brand more than they generate replies, and the person who was going to respond has already done so.

faq.q: Is WhatsApp appropriate for recruitment outreach?
faq.a: In India it is a normal and well-received channel when the message is relevant and clearly identifies you. In other markets it can read as intrusive. Match the channel to the market rather than to your own preference.

faq.q: Should you include salary in the first message?
faq.a: Including a band consistently improves reply quality, because it filters out mismatches before they cost anyone a call. Our channel response rates are measured on roles with strong compensation, and that is not a coincidence.

faq.q: Why is my recruitment outreach getting no replies?
faq.a: Usually the segment, not the copy. A precise segment with average wording outperforms brilliant wording sent to a broad list. If the positive reply rate is low while the raw reply rate is fine, the segment was wrong.

posts.title: High Volume Recruiting: What One Screening Day Actually Produces
posts.metaTitle: High Volume Recruiting: What One Day Produces
posts.description: A recruiter makes 40 calls a day and submits 3 or 4. What changes when 1,200 profiles are filtered to 300 contacts, and where the approach stops working.
posts.dek: A recruiter makes about 40 calls a day and finds 3 or 4 people worth submitting. Here is what changes when the pool is filtered first, and where the approach stops working.
posts.cardImageAlt: Staffing pipeline with candidates across stage columns, each showing a match score of 96, 93 or 92

toc.label: When it is the wrong approach

faq.q: How many calls can a recruiter make in a day?
faq.a: Around 40 on a full calling day, which on a good day converts to 3 or 4 candidates worth submitting. The ceiling is not dialling speed. It is that most of those 40 were never viable, and the recruiter finds that out one conversation at a time.

faq.q: How many candidates can be screened in a day with AI calling?
faq.a: In our own delivery, a filtered shortlist of roughly 300 people is contacted by call, email and WhatsApp in parallel, producing around 10 submission-ready profiles within a few hours. On a high-volume QA role we submitted 120 profiles in a single day, because the pool was deep and the criteria were wide.

faq.q: What roles suit high volume recruiting?
faq.a: Roles with clear, checkable eligibility criteria and a deep candidate pool. Volume QA, support, sales development and entry to mid engineering all work. Senior, confidential and executive searches do not, because the first conversation is a sell rather than a qualification.

faq.q: Does volume screening hurt candidate experience?
faq.a: It depends entirely on relevance and disclosure. A well-targeted call that respects someone's time performs better than a recruiter leaving 300 voicemails. A poorly targeted one at scale is worse than doing nothing, because you have annoyed 300 people instead of 40.

faq.q: How many profiles should you submit per role?
faq.a: Fewer than you can. Volume screening should produce a small evidenced shortlist, not a large list of everyone who passed. The exception is genuine high-volume hiring, where the client is filling many seats and wants breadth.

faq.q: What happens to candidates who do not make the shortlist?
faq.a: They return to the pool with a logged reason and freshly confirmed availability. That segment is the warmest list you own for the next similar role, which is the compounding argument for working your own database first.

posts.title: Recruitment CRM: What It Should Do Beyond Storing Names
posts.metaTitle: Recruitment CRM: What It Should Do Beyond Leads
posts.description: A staffing CRM has 3 jobs: win the client, deliver the role, collect the money. Most do one. What the other two require, from LinkedIn capture to the brief.
posts.dek: A staffing CRM has three jobs: win the client, deliver the role, collect the money. Most tools do the middle one and treat the other two as somebody else's problem.
posts.cardImageAlt: Contact record showing experience and company, with direct call, WhatsApp, LinkedIn and email actions

toc.label: What a CRM will not fix

faq.q: What is a recruitment CRM?
faq.a: A system that manages the client and prospect relationships that generate roles, as distinct from an ATS which manages candidates through a hiring process. Staffing firms need both, and running them as separate systems means the client brief gets retyped and the relationship history gets split.

faq.q: What is the difference between an ATS and a recruitment CRM?
faq.a: An ATS is organised around the requisition and closes the record when the role closes. A CRM is organised around the relationship, which outlives any individual role. The hiring manager who moves companies and the client who goes quiet for a year are both CRM problems that an ATS cannot hold.

faq.q: Can a recruitment CRM add leads from LinkedIn?
faq.a: Ours does, in one click from the profile, including fetching contact details and filing the person against the right company. The alternative is a recruiter copying a name into a spreadsheet, which is where most staffing business development quietly dies.

faq.q: Do staffing firms need a separate sales tool?
faq.a: Most do not, and the separation causes more problems than it solves. A generic sales CRM does not understand requisitions, submissions or placements, so the two systems end up being reconciled by hand every month.

faq.q: How does a CRM help with business development?
faq.a: By replacing a static prospect list with live signals. Researching which roles a company is currently hiring for turns a generic pitch into a specific one, and specificity is most of what separates a reply from a deletion.

faq.q: What is a staffing-specific notetaker?
faq.a: A meeting assistant that understands recruitment context, so a client call produces a structured brief with requirements, constraints and timelines rather than a generic transcript. The value is that the delivery team receives what the client actually said, not what the salesperson remembered.

posts.title: AI Interviews: How the Questions Are Built, What Gets Scored, and Where the Human Sits
posts.metaTitle: AI Interviews: How Questions Are Built and Scored
posts.description: AI interview questions built from 3 inputs: the job description, the weighted criteria and the company. What gets scored, and where the human must sit.
posts.dek: An AI interview is only as good as its questions, and most are drawn from a generic bank. Here is what changes when they come from the role's own criteria instead.
posts.cardImageAlt: Evaluation criteria screen showing generated criteria with descriptions and editable priority weights, plus a field for adding custom criteria

faq.q: How are AI interview questions generated?
faq.a: From three inputs: the job description, the weighted evaluation criteria for that role, and the company context. Each question traces back to something being assessed, which is what separates a role-specific interview from a generic question bank sorted by job title.

faq.q: Can an AI interview reject a candidate?
faq.a: It should not. The EU AI Act classifies recruitment AI as high-risk and requires human oversight of automated decisions. The workflow that holds up is the AI ranking and flagging, with a person making every rejection and every submission decision.

faq.q: Is AI interviewing legal?
faq.a: It is regulated rather than prohibited, and the requirements differ by jurisdiction. The EU AI Act, NYC Local Law 144, Illinois AIVIA and the Colorado AI Act all impose obligations around disclosure, bias auditing and human oversight. The rules follow the candidate's location, not your office's.

faq.q: What should an AI interview actually score?
faq.a: Verifiable facts such as notice period and compensation, evidenced claims about what someone built or owned, and inferred signals such as structure and domain fluency. The third group carries the least confidence and should carry the least weight, which is where most tools go wrong.

faq.q: How is an AI interview different from an AI screening call?
faq.a: A screening call qualifies: interest, availability, compensation and the CV claims that decide the submission. An interview assesses capability against the role's criteria in more depth. The first is about eligibility, the second is about fit.

faq.q: What is a good completion rate for an AI interview?
faq.a: There is no cross-industry standard worth relying on. Measure your own, segment it by role type and seniority, and treat a falling rate as a design problem rather than evidence of candidate quality. Candidates with the most options abandon first.

posts.title: Duplicate Candidate Records: Why They Happen, What They Cost, and How to Prevent Them
posts.metaTitle: Duplicate Candidate Records: Why They Happen and Cost
posts.description: In a 3 million record audit, about 10% were duplicates. How they enter, what email-based matching catches and misses, and what a merge has to preserve.
posts.dek: In a 3 million record audit at one firm, about 10% were duplicates. Here is how they enter, what identifier-based matching catches and misses, and what a merge has to preserve.
posts.cardImageAlt: Candidate record showing experience, current company, location, full career timeline and education on a single consolidated profile

faq.q: Why do duplicate candidate records happen?
faq.a: Four routes, all of them normal operations rather than mistakes: the same person applies to several roles over time, a recruiter uploads a CV without checking, a referral arrives with a different spelling or address, and bulk imports land without matching. Duplicates are a by-product of a working desk, not evidence of a careless one.

faq.q: How do you deduplicate a candidate database?
faq.a: By matching on an identifier at the point of entry rather than cleaning up later. We use email address as the unique key. That catches the common case cleanly, and it will not catch someone who applies from a work address and later a personal one, which is the main gap to plan around.

faq.q: What percentage of a staffing database is duplicated?
faq.a: In our audit of 3 million records at one firm, roughly 10% were duplicates and another 10% held no usable company information. Your own split will differ by firm age and hygiene, and a sample of 500 records is the only reliable way to establish it.

faq.q: How fast does candidate contact data go stale?
faq.a: Job titles and employers decay fastest, followed by work email addresses, then phone numbers. A candidate placed two years ago is very unlikely to hold the role your record states, which makes the record wrong rather than the person irrelevant.

faq.q: Should you delete old candidate records?
faq.a: Records with no reachable contact, no placement history and no recent activity cost more in search noise than they provide in value. Data protection law in most jurisdictions also requires a defensible retention position rather than indefinite storage, so deletion is a compliance step as well as a hygiene one.

faq.q: What should a merge preserve?
faq.a: Everything attached to every source record: notes, call and message history, attachments, submission and placement history, and stage changes with their timestamps. faq.a: Because a client with three usable CVs on Monday rarely waits for a fourth later in the week. Win rate is the entire business in a model where effort is spent before payment is certain, and being first has historically driven win rate.

faq.q: What replaces speed as a contingency differentiator?
faq.a: Accuracy. Client attention rather than client time is now the scarce resource. Submitting three candidates who all warrant an interview builds a reputation that submitting eight with two viable does not, and it compounds across roles.

faq.q: How do you win exclusivity on a role?
faq.a: With evidence rather than commitment. If your shortlists produce interviews at a materially higher rate than a client's other suppliers, exclusivity is a rational request. That requires tracking submission to interview ratio by client, which most firms do not.

faq.q: When should you decline a contingency role?
faq.a: When competition is high and the fee is low, when the skill is genuinely scarce enough to warrant retained terms, and when the client's approval chain is slow enough that your effort will sit unpaid indefinitely.

faq.q: Does AI make contingency recruiting more competitive?
faq.a: Initially yes, because more agencies can submit quickly. Over time it shifts the competition from speed to accuracy, which favours firms that verify properly rather than firms that simply move fast.

faq.q: Why do AI rollouts fail in staffing firms?
faq.a: Almost always on adoption rather than capability. Industry reporting shows a wide gap between firms claiming AI usage and firms with it genuinely embedded, and the cause is that teams were asked to change everything at once rather than one habit at a time.

faq.q: What should you enforce first in an AI rollout?
faq.a: One workflow, usually search. Every new role starts with a search of your own database before anybody opens a job portal. It is measurable, enforceable and produces a visible result within days, which is what buys the credibility for the next change.

faq.q: What is a good completion rate for an AI screening call?
faq.a: There is no reliable cross-industry benchmark. We see around 70 percent on calls of three to seven minutes. What matters more is measuring your own by seniority, since a rate that falls sharply at senior levels indicates a design problem rather than a candidate quality one.

faq.q: Do candidates dislike AI screening calls?

faq.q: Should you tell candidates a screening call is automated?
faq.a: Yes, before any questions are asked. It improves completion rather than harming it, because the alternative is a candidate realising mid-call and feeling misled. It is also a legal requirement in a growing number of jurisdictions.

faq.q: Why do strong candidates abandon automated screens?
faq.a: Because they have alternatives. Someone with three live processes will not spend twelve minutes on a speculative one, which means a poorly designed screen systematically filters out the strongest part of the market.

faq.q: What makes candidates complete an AI screening call?
faq.a: Keeping it short enough that every question traces to a real criterion, telling them at the start whether a person will see the results and when they will hear back, and making a human alternative visible even though few people use it.

faq.q: What should you measure besides completion rate?
faq.a: Completion by seniority, opt-out rate as volume changes, post-screen conversion, and any unprompted candidate feedback. High completion with low conversion means the screen is easy rather than useful.

faq.q: What is agentic AI in recruitment?
faq.a: A system given a goal rather than a path, which decides its own next action from context. This differs from a rule, which executes a decision somebody already made, and from a workflow, which chains rules along a route designed in advance.

faq.q: What is the difference between automation and AI in recruiting?
faq.a: Automation executes predetermined steps. A rule fires on a condition and a workflow chains rules in a designed sequence. An agent chooses what to do given an objective, which is why it can handle situations nobody configured.

faq.q: Is agentic AI better than workflow automation?
faq.a: For handling cases outside the configured path, yes. For predictability and auditability, workflows are stronger. Recruiting produces unanticipated cases constantly, which is where workflow automation quietly turns exception handling into the recruiter's main job.

faq.q: Where does agentic AI fail in recruitment?
faq.a: It is less predictable than a rule, which matters in compliance contexts. It needs a clear goal, so a badly briefed role produces confident action in the wrong direction. And it still requires human oversight of decisions.

faq.q: How do you tell whether a vendor has agents or workflows?
faq.a: Ask them to demonstrate the system handling a case nobody configured, and ask who decided the path. A workflow escalates to a human when something unexpected happens; an agent acts on it.

faq.q: Do AI agents need human oversight in hiring?
faq.a: Yes. Under the EU AI Act's high-risk classification for recruitment systems, human oversight of automated decisions is a legal obligation rather than a matter of good practice.

faq.q: How is temp staffing different from professional recruitment?
faq.a: Speed to fill matters more than quality of fill, because an unfilled shift is unrecoverable revenue rather than a delay. Quality is a threshold to clear rather than a scale to optimise, which inverts how most recruiting tools are designed.

faq.q: What is redeployment and why does it matter?
faq.a: Placing a worker into a new assignment as their current one ends. It is the cheapest placement available since the worker is known, compliant and needs no sourcing, and it is usually missed because nobody acts on end dates until they arrive.

faq.q: Why do temp candidates get contacted multiple times?
faq.a: Usually because the same person exists more than once in the database, so several recruiters legitimately work separate records. Matching at the point of entry fixes it; periodic cleanup does not.

faq.q: How fast does temp worker availability change?
faq.a: Within days rather than weeks. Someone available on Monday may have taken a shift by Wednesday, which makes automated re-confirmation across a pool the highest-value automation available on this desk type.

faq.q: Can AI fill shifts automatically?
faq.a: It can confirm availability across a large pool, rank who is reachable and contact them in parallel, which is most of the work. Compliance checks and no-show management remain human responsibilities with real consequences.

faq.q: What should a temp desk measure?
faq.a: Fill rate against shifts released, redeployment rate on assignments ending, and time from shift release to confirmed worker. Sourcing volume tells you very little on this desk type.

faq.q: Why are clients pushing back on agency fees?

faq.q: What can a staffing agency do that a client's internal team cannot?

faq.q: What is outcome-based pricing in IT services?
faq.a: A contract where the client pays for a defined result rather than for time and materials. The vendor decides how many people it takes and absorbs the delivery risk, which reverses the incentive to maximise billable headcount.

faq.q: How does outcome pricing affect bench hiring?
faq.a: A bench stops being recoverable inventory and becomes overhead. Firms carry smaller benches, hire closer to the requirement with less notice, and use contract labour for the variable portion to convert fixed cost into variable.

faq.q: Why does quality per hire matter more under outcome contracts?
faq.a: Because the cost of a weak hire lands on the vendor rather than the client. Someone needing six weeks of supervision consumes a senior engineer's time and the project margin, which is visible immediately rather than absorbed in billable hours.

faq.q: What should staffing firms change for outcome-driven clients?
faq.a: Verify capability rather than availability, expect tighter specifications with fewer seats, price on difficulty rather than volume, and sell to the person who owns the delivery outcome rather than to procurement.

faq.q: Does outcome pricing reduce demand for contract staff?
faq.a: Generally the opposite. Firms avoiding permanent commitments use contract labour for the variable portion of delivery, which increases contingent demand even as speculative bench hiring falls.

faq.q: Has all of IT services moved to outcome pricing?
faq.a: No. Time and materials remains a large share of the market, and firms running both models behave differently depending on which contract a role sits under. It is worth asking which applies before assuming the brief.

faq.q: How is GCC hiring different from IT staffing?

faq.q: Who does a staffing firm compete with on GCC work?
faq.a: The client's own internal talent team, which is usually capable and well-tooled. Your submission timeline is benchmarked against theirs rather than against other agencies, which makes throughput the commercial argument.

faq.a: Not if the supply genuinely does not exist. If forty people in the country can do the job, a faster process reaches the same forty. That is search work and should be priced accordingly rather than delivered as volume.

faq.q: What skills should a recruiter have in 2026?
faq.a: Specification, triage judgement, selling and client conversation. If sourcing and first-pass screening are automated, the remaining job is deciding what to do with results and persuading people, both of which are judgement rather than process.

faq.q: Is Boolean search still a useful hiring criterion?

faq.a: Hand them a real brief and ask what they would reject on, give them five candidate summaries with sixty seconds each to triage, role-play a candidate with a competing offer, and ask them to explain a market they claim to know.

faq.q: Can you hire recruiters from outside recruitment?
faq.a: Increasingly, yes. If the job is judgement, specification and selling rather than syntax and stamina, then sales, account management and domain specialists bring what matters and lack only process knowledge, which is teachable.

faq.a: Resilience and follow-through. Recruitment involves being told no repeatedly by both sides, and the gap between offer and joining is entirely human work where a candidate going quiet needs a person rather than a workflow.

faq.q: What is a VMS in staffing?
faq.a: A vendor management system is software the client uses to manage its contingent workforce and its supplier base. Requisitions are released to suppliers through it, candidates are submitted back through it, and rate cards are enforced automatically.

faq.q: What is the difference between a VMS and an MSP?
faq.a: A VMS is the software. An MSP is a managed service provider that runs the programme on the client's behalf, sitting between the client and the suppliers. Many programmes involve both.

faq.q: How do vendor management programmes affect agency margins?
faq.a: They make suppliers comparable on rate while making candidate quality invisible at the point of comparison, enforce published rate cards, and frequently pass a programme fee to the supplier. Aggregate temp staffing gross margin sits near 21 percent.

faq.q: What is supplier tiering?
faq.a: Programmes release requisitions to tier one suppliers first for a defined window, then to lower tiers. A tier-two supplier therefore works roles tier one could not fill, at the same rate card, which is a worse requisition mix at the same price.

faq.q: Can you negotiate rates inside a VMS programme?
faq.a: Rarely, since programmes exist specifically to prevent per-supplier negotiation. Tier movement, earned by reliably filling the requisitions the programme struggles with, is the route that actually responds.

faq.q: When should a staffing firm leave a VMS programme?
faq.a: When fill rate inside the programme is materially below fill rate outside it, which indicates adverse selection, or when programme work becomes a majority of revenue and the client effectively sets your margin and risk profile.

faq.q: What is the best commission structure for recruiters?
faq.a: One that pays on margin where margin can be measured, uses a rolling period rather than a calendar month to reduce timing games, pays something explicit for account development, and states clearly what happens when somebody leaves.

faq.q: Why do monthly billing targets cause problems?
faq.a: Because a placement landing next quarter is worth nothing this month, which produces deal timing games, under-investment in accounts that pay later, and abandonment of anything that will not convert quickly.

faq.q: Are team-based commission pools a good idea?

faq.a: Directly. Who is credited when a candidate sourced years ago is placed today, or when one person owns the client and another the candidate, is a payment question. Configuring permissions before writing the policy means a vendor default sets your compensation.

faq.q: Why do commission plans fail to motivate?
faq.a: Frequently because they were designed to be affordable rather than motivating. A high threshold with a modest rate is cost control described as an incentive, and recruiters read that accurately within a quarter.

faq.q: What should you measure on a recruitment desk?
faq.a: Ratios rather than counts. Submission to interview, interview to offer, offer to join, and time from brief to first submission. A ratio cannot be improved by doing more low-quality work, which is what makes it resistant to gaming.

faq.q: Why should staffing firms measure roles declined?
faq.a: Because a recruiter who works every requirement offered is demonstrating an inability to qualify rather than commitment. Measuring it gives permission to conclude a role is not worth working, which changes intake behaviour immediately.

faq.q: How often should recruitment metrics be reviewed?
faq.a: Monthly for ratio metrics, since they are noisy over shorter periods and weekly review produces reaction rather than management. Daily review suits leading indicators such as time to first submission.

faq.q: Is AI resume screening useful?
faq.a: In a narrow way. It decides who gets a conversation faster. It does not qualify anybody, because the claims that decide a submission cannot be tested by a document, and reading CVs was never the constraint on a staffing desk.

faq.q: Why is resume screening a crowded software category?
faq.a: Because it is the easiest capability to build: the input is text, the output is a number, the ranking is subjective enough that nobody can prove it wrong, and it demos well. Crowding signals difficulty rather than value.

faq.q: Has AI made CVs less reliable?
faq.a: Yes. Tailoring a CV to mirror a job description now takes seconds, so the document reflects the posting more than the candidate. Every application matches on keywords, which makes ranking them an exercise in scoring tool usage.

faq.q: What does a good resume screening tool do differently?
faq.a: Scores against criteria generated from that specific job description with adjustable weights, shows the reasoning behind every score so a recruiter can interrogate it, and acts as a filter for who gets a conversation rather than as a rejection decision.

faq.q: Should a resume screener reject candidates automatically?
faq.a: No. Under the EU AI Act's high-risk classification for recruitment systems, human oversight of automated decisions is an obligation. Beyond compliance, a client rejecting a shortlist wants a person who can explain the reasoning.

faq.q: What should a staffing firm buy instead of a resume screener?
faq.a: Search that makes an existing database findable, qualification by conversation at volume, and automatic capture of calls and messages onto the record. All three move a number rather than accelerating the path to the same conversation.

faq.q: Are job boards still worth it for staffing firms?

faq.q: What does AI-native actually mean in recruiting software?
faq.a: That the product was designed assuming the model exists rather than having capability added later. Concretely: search that takes a description rather than a query, screening that runs as a conversation, criteria generated from a brief, and records that write themselves.

faq.q: How do you tell real AI from AI washing?

faq.q: Why is AI capability often on a higher pricing tier?
faq.a: Because architecture rarely ships as an upsell. When a capability is genuinely in the path that data travels through, it tends to be part of the product. Capability priced as an add-on is more often bolted on.

faq.q: What is the fastest way to test an AI claim?
faq.a: Ask the vendor to demonstrate the system handling something nobody configured for, such as an ambiguous candidate reply. A workflow escalates to a human; genuine capability acts on it.

faq.q: Should AI features influence a software purchase?
faq.a: Only the load-bearing ones. Message drafting and CV summarisation are general model calls that every competitor will match. Search, screening and evaluation built into the data model are a different investment.

faq.q: Why do diverse shortlists not change hiring outcomes?
faq.a: Because composition is decided upstream. By the time a shortlist is assembled the pool has already been filtered by where the role was advertised, how it was written and who was sourced. A ratio applied at that point rearranges survivors.

faq.q: What is requirement inflation in hiring?
faq.a: Criteria that are stated as requirements but are not actually required: a specific institution tier, continuous employment, or a years figure standing in as a proxy. They are usually written without intent and they filter unevenly.

faq.q: How do you test whether a requirement is genuine?
faq.a: Ask what happens if a candidate does not have it. If the honest answer is that they could still do the job, it is a preference rather than a gate and should be weighted rather than used to exclude.

faq.q: Does structured evaluation reduce bias?
faq.a: It reduces variance between assessors, which is worth having. It does not correct a biased input, and any scoring configured on past outcomes can reproduce the pattern in them, which is why bias auditing is a regulatory requirement in several jurisdictions.

faq.q: What is the difference between a perm and a contract desk?
faq.a: A perm placement is a single event billed on start. A contract placement is an annuity billed for the life of the assignment. That cascades into cash flow, recruiter activity, client relationship dynamics and how each desk should be measured.

faq.q: Why does contract staffing consume cash?
faq.a: Because you pay workers on a shorter cycle than clients pay you. A contract desk growing quickly consumes working capital even while profitable, which is why firms can run out of money during their strongest quarter.

faq.q: Can the same recruiter work perm and contract roles?
faq.a: Usually poorly. Perm rewards depth per candidate and long client process management; contract rewards speed and availability-driven decisions. Most people are meaningfully better at one, and mixing them produces predictable failures in both directions.

faq.q: What is redeployment and why does it matter?
faq.a: Moving a contractor to a new assignment as the current one ends. It is the cheapest revenue on a contract desk since there is no sourcing cost or compliance rework, and it is missed because firms act on end dates only when they arrive.

faq.q: Should perm and contract have separate targets?
faq.a: Yes. A single revenue target pushes recruiters towards whichever pays faster this month, which is usually perm, and the contract book stops being fed. Margin should also be reported separately since spread and perm gross margin are different numbers.

faq.q: Which desk is more valuable when selling a staffing firm?
faq.a: Contract revenue is generally valued above perm because it is more predictable, in the same way recurring software revenue is valued above project services. Concentration risk on contract accounts is more visible, which cuts the other way.

faq.q: How do you plan a 1,000-seat hiring ramp?
faq.a: Work backwards from the required joiners through acceptance rate, interview conversion, submission rate and contact rate to establish the top-of-funnel requirement. That arithmetic in week one determines whether the mandate is deliverable at all.

faq.q: What is the main constraint in volume hiring?
faq.a: Screening throughput. Sourcing at volume is comparatively easy; qualifying at volume caps the project. A recruiter running manual screening manages around 40 calls a day and finds three or four people worth submitting.

faq.q: Why do large hiring ramps stall?
faq.a: Frequently because the client cannot process the volume. If they can interview thirty a day, submitting three hundred creates a backlog, a poor candidate experience and a queue of people who take other jobs while waiting.

faq.q: What is offer-to-join leakage on volume hiring?
faq.a: The share of candidates who accept an offer and do not turn up. It runs higher on volume ramps than on individual placements and it needs to be built into the plan from day one rather than discovered in week four.

faq.q: How do you prevent quality drift on a ramp?
faq.a: By defining the bar as explicit weighted criteria rather than as a general standard, so that any relaxation is visible rather than gradual. Drift is usually invisible until client attrition surfaces it months later.

faq.q: What should you agree with the client before a volume mandate?
faq.a: Interview capacity per day with a named owner, decision turnaround in hours, the quality bar defined as criteria, what happens if the client stalls, and replacement terms specific to the ramp cohort.

faq.q: How do you fill a role when very few people can do it?
faq.a: Establish first whether it is genuinely scarce by mapping the market against capability rather than title. If supply really is dozens, the job becomes being answered rather than being thorough, and preparing the client for a trade-off on compensation, location or adjacency.

faq.q: What makes healthcare staffing different from other staffing?

faq.a: In adjacent skills. Data engineers and backend engineers working on inference infrastructure are frequently better hires for AI-adjacent roles than people carrying the title, because engineering fundamentals are harder to teach than the domain.

faq.q: Why do technical requisitions stay open for months?
faq.a: Usually because the decision has not been made rather than because the market is thin. Client behaviour is bimodal: certain clients move in days, uncertain ones do not move at all while the role remains technically open.

faq.a: Referral remains the highest-yield channel at senior levels. Compensation remains the most common reason offers fail. And counter-offers still succeed often enough that the period between acceptance and joining deserves as much attention as the search.

faq.q: What is the best sourcing channel for blue collar hiring in India?

faq.q: Why is upselling existing clients cheaper than winning new ones?
faq.a: Because the client costs nothing to acquire, already trusts you and understands how you work. The credibility that takes months to build with a new logo already exists, which makes expansion the highest-margin revenue available.

faq.q: How do you find expansion opportunities inside a client?
faq.a: By mapping the organisation first: how many people it employs, which functions hire regularly, who runs each and what the headcount plan is. Without that map, expansion is opportunistic and depends on someone mentioning a role.

faq.q: When is the best time to ask a client for more work?

faq.q: Should you ask a client for more roles or for an introduction?
faq.a: An introduction. Asking whether they have other roles usually ends the conversation, since they often do not. Asking to be introduced to a peer who is hiring is a smaller favour they can grant immediately.

faq.q: What stops staffing firms from expanding inside accounts?
faq.a: Usually three internal obstacles: the account owner is a delivery person who was never asked to sell, nobody is accountable for account growth with a target, and the commission plan does not pay for work that produces revenue later.

faq.q: What should you measure to track expansion headroom?
faq.a: Functions served versus functions available inside each client. That single ratio shows how much of an account is unworked, and almost no staffing firm tracks it.

faq.q: What should a recruiter commission plan pay on?
faq.a: Margin where it can be measured, since a flat percentage of billings makes a recruiter indifferent between a high-margin difficult placement and two easy low-margin ones. Activity counts should be avoided because every count can be raised by lowering the standard.

faq.q: Should commission be paid monthly or on a rolling period?
faq.a: A twelve-week rolling window removes most deal timing games, where placements are pulled forward or pushed back depending on where a recruiter sits against a monthly target. It costs some simplicity and removes month-end behaviour.

faq.q: How do you pay recruiters for account development?
faq.a: With a small explicit component separate from placement commission, a retrospective bonus when an account crosses a revenue threshold, or protected time. Expecting it as professionalism does not work, because it costs billing time and earns nothing.

faq.q: What edge cases must a commission plan address?
faq.a: Ownership disputes over candidates sourced years earlier, split placements where one person owns the client and another the candidate, what is paid on placements in flight when somebody resigns, and clawbacks when a placement fails inside the guarantee period.

faq.q: Why do commission plans fail to motivate?
faq.a: Frequently because they are designed to be affordable and then described as motivating. A high threshold with a modest rate is cost control, and recruiters read that accurately within a quarter.

faq.q: Should you test a commission plan before launching it?
faq.a: Yes. Show it to two recruiters before it goes live. They will identify the gaming route within ten minutes, which is considerably cheaper than discovering it after a quarter of results.

faq.q: How does a return to office mandate affect hiring?
faq.a: It applies a geographic filter before any skills filter, reducing the pool to people within commuting distance plus the few willing to relocate. On specialist requirements that can turn a workable search into a genuinely scarce one.

faq.q: Does an office mandate change who applies or just how many?
faq.a: Both. The pool filters disproportionately on caregivers, people with long commutes, people managing health conditions and those who relocated during the remote period, which shifts composition as well as volume.

faq.q: Why is hybrid a problematic term in job postings?
faq.a: Because it covers arrangements from four days in office to two days a month. Candidates discount the word entirely, so a posting that does not specify days produces both wasted applications and lost candidates.

faq.q: What do candidates trade against office attendance?
faq.a: Commute time more than salary. A one-hour each-way commute is roughly two working days a month, which most people price above a modest compensation difference. Predictability of days also matters more than the number of them.

faq.q: How should an agency raise workplace policy with a client?
faq.a: With two search results rather than an opinion: the pool with the location constraint and without it. Then name the composition effect factually and ask what the mandate is actually for, since some purposes have alternatives.

faq.q: Can workplace policy conflict with diversity objectives?
faq.a: It frequently does without anyone connecting the two, since an office mandate filters disproportionately on groups a diversity objective is trying to reach. Raising it as a factual observation about supply is more useful than framing it as a policy argument.

faq.q: How is dual employment detected in India?
faq.a: Usually through statutory records rather than investigation. Provident fund contributions link to a universal account number that follows an individual, so contributions from two employers in the same period are visible in the record.

faq.q: Is moonlighting illegal in India?
faq.a: There is no blanket prohibition on holding more than one job. The position is contractual: some employment contracts prohibit it outright, some permit it with prior written disclosure, and some are silent on the matter.

faq.q: Why is dual employment a staffing firm's problem?
faq.a: Because it usually surfaces after the candidate has joined, when the client has already paid the fee and invested in onboarding. The conversation that follows is about your screening standard rather than the candidate's judgement.

faq.q: Should recruiters ask candidates about other engagements?
faq.a: Yes, at screening rather than at offer, framed factually rather than as an integrity test. Most candidates answer honestly when asked plainly, and a disclosure at screening can be managed with the client rather than becoming a problem later.

faq.q: Does a notice period overlap count as dual employment?
faq.a: Not necessarily. A candidate serving notice while a new employer begins contributions can produce a technical overlap that is entirely legitimate, and treating it as a red flag creates unnecessary escalation.

faq.q: What should a staffing firm record about dual employment?
faq.a: Current engagements as a structured field captured at screening, the client's own policy captured at intake, and evidence that the question was asked. That record is the difference between a delivery failure and a disclosed risk the client accepted.

faq.q: What do pay transparency laws require?
faq.a: Broadly, that salary ranges are disclosed on job postings or provided on request, with the detail varying by jurisdiction. Several US states, EU member states implementing the pay transparency directive, and other markets have introduced requirements.

faq.q: How do pay transparency laws affect staffing agencies?
faq.a: They remove an information asymmetry that was part of the intermediary's value. The agency knew what the client would pay and what the candidate would accept; when the range is public, value has to come from market knowledge instead.

faq.q: Why do published salary ranges get so wide?
faq.a: Because a broad band technically complies while preserving employer flexibility. The consequence is that candidates anchor to the top, employers intend the middle, and the gap surfaces at offer stage after weeks of process.

faq.q: Should recruiters still ask candidates about salary expectations?
faq.a: It works less well once the range is public, since the candidate already knows it and the question reads as an attempt to anchor low. The more useful conversation moves to fit, which is what money was previously doing work to obscure.

faq.q: Why do clients post conservative salary ranges?
faq.a: Because their existing employees can see the posting. A band above what current staff earn creates an internal equity problem, so employers post conservatively, which can constrain what they offer externally below market rate.

faq.q: What should agencies capture at intake now?
faq.a: Both the published range and the client's actual expectation for the profile described, as separate fields. They differ more often than not, and the difference determines which candidates are worth approaching.

faq.q: Does the EU AI Act apply to recruitment?
faq.a: Yes. AI used for recruitment, candidate selection and evaluation is classified as high-risk, which brings transparency, human oversight, record-keeping and bias management obligations rather than an outright prohibition.

faq.q: Does the EU AI Act apply to a staffing firm outside the EU?
faq.a: It applies where the output of the AI system is used within the EU. An agency placing candidates into EU-based roles or for EU employers should plan as though it is in scope, regardless of where its recruiters sit.

faq.q: Can AI reject candidates automatically under the EU AI Act?
faq.a: Human oversight of automated decisions is required, which means a person must be able to review, override and take responsibility. A workflow where a system rejects without human review is the specific arrangement the rules target.

faq.q: What is the difference between a provider and a deployer?
faq.a: A provider builds the AI system and carries the heavier obligations around conformity, documentation and testing. A deployer uses it and is typically responsible for intended use, human oversight, candidate disclosure and records of use.

faq.q: Do candidates have to be told AI is being used?
faq.a: Transparency obligations mean people should know when AI is used in a process assessing them, stated before the assessment rather than afterwards. This is also good practice, since disclosure tends to improve completion rather than reduce it.

faq.q: What should a staffing firm ask its ATS vendor about the AI Act?
faq.a: For documentation on bias auditing, how scores are produced and can be explained, what data is retained and for how long, and whether the vendor considers itself a provider under the Act. A vendor who cannot answer is a risk you carry.

faq.q: Does the DPDP Act apply to recruitment databases?
faq.a: A candidate database is personal data at scale, so the framework's requirements around purpose, lawful basis and retention apply to it. Staffing firms are more exposed than internal talent teams because reuse across clients and years is the business model.

faq.q: How long can a staffing firm keep candidate data?

faq.q: Who is responsible for contract labour compliance in India?
faq.a: Obligations split between the contractor supplying workers, who typically requires a licence and carries wage and statutory contribution duties, and the principal employer engaging them, who requires registration and is responsible for ensuring the contractor complies.

faq.q: What is principal employer liability?
faq.a: If a contractor fails to make required statutory payments, the principal employer can be required to make good the shortfall and recover it from the contractor. This gives your client direct financial exposure to your compliance.

faq.q: Why do enterprise clients audit staffing suppliers?
faq.a: Because they carry liability for supplier failures. Vendor onboarding asking for licence copies, contribution records and register extracts is the client protecting itself rather than administrative caution.

faq.q: Where do staffing firms most often fail on compliance?
faq.a: Statutory contributions filed late during cash flow pressure, licence thresholds crossed as the firm grows without the position being reviewed, registers not kept current, and worker classification that does not match the actual arrangement.

faq.q: What documents should a staffing agency keep current?
faq.a: Current licence with the threshold position documented, principal employer registration status, statutory contribution records with evidence of remittance, wage registers, attendance and hours records, and worker-level identity and certification documentation.

faq.q: Is back office a compliance function in contract staffing?
faq.a: Effectively yes. Hours worked, wages paid and contributions remitted with their dates are the evidence base a compliance audit examines, which is why data scattered across spreadsheets and providers becomes a liability under audit.
